..
KEY MESSAGE 1...

West to northwest flow aloft continues over NY and New 
England with a mid and upper level trough over the Northeast. 500
hPa temps are about -13C based on the 12Z sounding from KALY. 
Temps are near to slightly cooler than normal. Dewpoints 
continue to be in the upper 50s to mid 60s. MLCAPE values based 
on the 17-18Z SPC RAP analysis are in 500-1000 J/kg range over 
eastern NY and western New England. 500 hPa winds are around 50 
KT, so the 0-6 km bulk shear is 50-60 KT, but there is a lot of 
dry air aloft. Also, the mid level lapse rates are generally 
less than 6C/km. We are also located on the unfavorable right 
exit region of the mid/upper level jet streak. Updrafts may not 
become tall enough for a robust severe threat, unless a rogue 
severe cell occurs tapping into more instability. However, with 
the strong 700-500 hPa winds some gusty winds /35-50 mph/ or 
sub-severe hail under penny-size could occur especially from the
Capital Region north and east into the Berkshires and southern 
VT. Near normal PWATs around an inch with fast steering winds 
aloft should reduce any hydro threat. The showers/thunderstorms 
should diminish quickly by sunset with the skies becoming mostly
clear to partly cloudy with a sfc high ridging in from the 
Lower Great Lakes Region. Some radiational mist/fog may form 
north of Albany in the Upper Hudson Valley, also in the Mohawk 
Valley, narrow valleys in the southwest Adirondacks and east of 
the southern Greens where patchy fog was added. Some residual 
clouds may inhibit fog formation further south. Low temps fall 
into the 50s with some upper 40s over the southern Greens and 
the Adirondack Park. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Another impulse in the west to northwest flow moves across eastern 
NY and western New England tomorrow. The deep shear in the 0-6
km continues to be strong at 50-60 KT. The residual cold pool 
aloft coupled with weak or modest instability with the latest 
HREFs showing mean SBCAPEs mainly less than 500 J/kg should 
allow for a slight to low chance for a brief shower or 
thunderstorm. PoPs were kept mainly in the slight to low chance 
range range. Again, the limited instability should inhibit any 
severe threat and the thunderstorms are not expected to be 
severe, as we agree with general thunderstorm forecast from SPC.
Breezy northwest winds should allow dewpoints to fall into the 
50s to lower 60s and high temps will be near to slightly below 
normal with mid 60s to mid 70s over the hills and mtns, and 
upper 70s to lower 80s in the valleys. rain or greater, so will 
continue to monitor model QPF trends.

KEY MESSAGE 3...
The skies will become mostly clear/clear with a 
surface anticyclone building in from southeast Ontario. Some 
patchy radiational mist/fog will likely develop in the major river 
valleys.  Lows will fall into the mid 40s to mid 50s across the 
forecast area, as we trended closer to the cooler MAVMOS values. 
Would not be surprised if a few readings in the west/southwest 
Adirondacks fall close to 40F. After a chilly start for mid-
August, temps rebound into the upper 60s to upper 70s (slightly
below normal) across the forecast area with mostly sunny 
conditions due to the strong sfc high building in overhead. 
Humidity levels will be pleasant for mid-August. 

Low and mid level heights fall Sat night into Sun, as a low 
pressure approaches from the Great Lakes Region and Ohio. Mid 
and high clouds increase Sat night, as it will not be quite as 
cool as the previous night. Low and mid-level warm advection 
increases ahead of the approaching wave and warm front for 
showers to increase in the late morning into the afternoon from 
west to east. PoPs were continued in the likely to categorical 
range (55-85%) from the afternoon into the early evening. 
Periods of rain with a few thunderstorms continue into the 
overnight. PWATs rise back above normal. The latest NBM 
indicates that the 24-hr probabilities for >0.50" of rainfall 
ending 12Z/Mon are in 50-70% range across eastern NY and 
western New England. The chances for >1" of rainfall for the 
24-hr period ending that same time frame are 25-40%. The 
rainfall continues Sun night into Mon morning, as a secondary 
wave may form near Long Island/southern New England. WPC 
continues a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) in the Excessive 
Rainfall graphic, so we will have to monitor for some heavier 
rainfall elements that may cause some ponding of water on 
roadways or poor drainage flooding of low-lying areas. Temps 
continue to run cooler than normal to close the weekend with the
increasing clouds and rain cooled air.
